->### OF MR. LEIBNITZ. ###<-

(i) 7
<meta>catchword: mand</meta>

...that he persuaded himself he had found in his philosophy a means to explain the Presence of Jesus Christ in the <term>Eucharist</term> <note>The Eucharist, or Holy Communion, is the Christian rite commemorating the Last Supper; Leibniz sought a philosophical explanation that might satisfy both Protestant and Catholic views on the real presence of Christ.</note>, according to the ideas of the theologians of his party <note>Leibniz was a Lutheran, though he frequently corresponded with scholars of all denominations.</note>.

It is true that he did not go much to public assemblies of devotion; but does this external worship alone characterize religion? How many idle people of either sex, who in all places make a regular pastime of attending church, and who without this aid would be quite embarrassed by their own figure, and plunged into a mortal boredom? How many others are drawn there only by vanity, by false devotion, and perhaps by even more shameful passions? Great diligence in attending church is therefore no more a proof of religion than a rarer attendance would be of irreligion; and all things considered, Mr. Leibniz would only become blameworthy for having neglected an external duty and ceremonial rites.

Common rumors against him never serve as proof. Since he was very moderate in relation to the three religions that dominate in the Empire <note>The Holy Roman Empire, which at the time officially recognized three "confessions": Catholicism, Lutheranism, and Calvinism (the Reformed Church).</note>, and because he greatly esteemed several Jesuits and their learned Society in general, some Catholics flattered themselves with the hope of being able to win him over, especially when he was made <term>Aulic Councilor</term> <note>A high-ranking legal and political advisor in the court of the Holy Roman Emperor in Vienna.</note> and when he came to Vienna; but as soon as they saw him return to Hanover, they began to lose this hope, and a certain German play on words was then made about him

It once happened that Mr. Leibniz feigned a devotion in which he certainly placed no belief. Here is the fact (*b*). One day, during one of his travels on the Italian sea, a furious storm arose; the disconcerted Pilot—who did not think he was being understood by a German whom he regarded as the cause of the storm, judging him a heretic—proposed throwing him into the sea. <margin>He is also accused of avarice.</margin>
Mr. Leibniz is also accused of avarice. It would be better to say that he should have lived in a less economical manner, and sought out more of the comforts of well-being which his income allowed him to procure. Furthermore (said Mr. De Fontenelle <note>Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle (1657–1757), a French author and influential perpetual secretary of the Academy of Sciences, who wrote a famous eulogy for Leibniz.</note> on this subject, whose reflections have so often decorated this Draft), he let the management of his household go as his Servants pleased, and he spent much through negligence.

<margin>Regarding his reputation for Projects.</margin>
Mr. Leibniz, it is said, took pleasure in forming a great number of Projects that he never completed, and for which his life and the lives of several people together would not have sufficed. However, there are no skilled people who do not find themselves in this situation. Genius and knowledge provide more visions—even inspiring a more enterprising courage—than the human condition allows; and perhaps one would not do all that one can without the hope of doing more than one is able. Success in the Sciences, as in the affairs of civil life, is often only the reward for a certain boldness. There are types of rashness that can only come from great Masters. If he had not accomplished so much, one could place his projects among the Chimera <note>original: *Chimeres*, referring to impossible or illusory schemes or idle fantasies.</note> with which some Men of Letters have lulled the Public.

<summary>This page defends Leibniz against charges of greed and impracticality, arguing that his "avarice" was merely household neglect and his "unfinished projects" were the necessary byproduct of a daring, visionary genius.</summary>

<margin>Of his desire to be seen as one of the foremost Scholars.</margin>
Mr. Leibniz was extremely sensitive to the passion for being regarded by other men as one of the foremost Scholars of his century. This much is admitted. But do his works not justify this sensitivity? Indeed, an ardor for study naturally suggests a man eager for glory. For after all, for all the sleepless nights he endures, can he aim for any rewards other than praise and esteem? It is the flattering hope of being held in high regard that serves as a spur to virtue. Those who are not touched by it always crawl, lost within the crowd, while those who are sustained by this noble ambition rise above their peers and march with giant strides upon the path to immortality.

But, some add, Mr. Leibniz pushed vanity too far on this point, and particularly regarding his works and discoveries. The pains and cares one takes, the love of what one has found, and the sweetness of securing its possession, could almost serve him as quite legitimate excuses.

<margin>Finally, of having become a Courtier.</margin>
Finally, he is reproached for having subsequently abandoned this passion for the Muses <note>In this context, the "Muses" represents the pursuit of the arts, sciences, and literature.</note>, and for having sought, during the final years of his life, to be more of a Courtier than a Philosopher. This would then be a weakness difficult to justify. Let us leave it to those who saw and knew him at that time to pronounce on the validity of this accusation. If it is found to be well-founded, it is appar-

### XXVI. *

G. W. L. <note>G. G. L. in the original text stands for Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, using the Latinized "Guilielmus."</note> *A brief demonstration of a memorable error by Descartes and others regarding the Law of Nature, according to which they maintain that the same quantity of motion is always preserved by God, a principle they also misapply in mechanics; communicated in a letter dated January 6.* <note>original Latin: "Brevis Demonstratio erroris memorabilis Cartesii & aliorum circa Legem Naturæ..." This is one of Leibniz's most famous papers, where he challenged the Cartesian view of physics.</note>

Leipzig Journal. March 1686. page 161. This Demonstration is in French, and followed by a Reply, in the *News from the Republic of Letters* September 1686. page 996.

A question is raised in Physics: should the Force of a Body in Impact be measured by the product of its Mass and its Velocity, or by the product of the Mass and the Square of the Velocity? <note>This refers to the "Vis Viva" (living force) controversy. Descartes believed the universe's total "quantity of motion" ($mv$) remained constant. Leibniz argued that the true conserved quantity was what we now call kinetic energy ($mv^2$).</note> This is a famous question that still divides all Physicists! It is the second method of estimating the Force of Impact of Bodies that Mr. Leibniz proposes here, a matter on which Mr. Newton has taken the opposite view. Both have found great and zealous partisans; and what will appear even more singular, they have found Geometers <note>In this period, "Geometer" was often used to mean a high-level mathematician or mathematical physicist.</note> of the first rank who speak only after performing Experiments. A detailed history of this single dispute would form an entire Work. But it will suffice to say for the present that on one side, all of England—and in particular Drs. Clarke, Pemberton, and Desaguliers—have loudly declared for Mr. Newton; on the other, Mr. Hermann, Mr. Wolff, the Marquis Poleni, and Mr. 's Gravesande have taken the side of Mr. Leibniz.

It identifies the major European scientists who took sides in this foundational debate of classical mechanics.</summary>

G. G. L. *A Small Addition to the Considerations of Ferdinand Helfrich Lichtscheid.* <note>original Latin: "Additatiuncula ad Considerationes Ferdin. Helfrici Lichtscheid." Lichtscheid was a contemporary mathematician and theologian.</note>
Leipzig Journal. Octob. 1691. page 500.

### XLI.

*On Religious Tolerance. Letters from Mr. Leibniz, & Responses from Mr. Pellisson.* Paris 1692. in 12mo.

This small work was first reprinted in Holland; in it, Mr. Leibniz approves of Tolerance, & Mr. Pellisson <note>Paul Pellisson was a prominent French author and convert to Catholicism who engaged in a famous series of exchanges with Leibniz regarding the potential reunification of the Protestant and Catholic churches.</note> rejects it. The Letters of these two Gentlemen on this subject are inserted in part in the *Otium Hannoveranum*. <note>A collection of Leibniz's miscellaneous papers and correspondence, published posthumously.</note> There reigns a great deal of good faith, politeness, & charity on both sides. Furthermore, they have only lightly touched upon this matter, which skilled people, and especially in England, have so well deepened that they have exhausted it. <note>This likely refers to English thinkers like John Locke, whose "Letter Concerning Toleration" (1689) had recently set the standard for the debate.</note>

### XLIII. *

*On the Catenary; or Solution to the famous Problem proposed by Galileo, to serve as an Essay for a new Analysis of Infinities, with its use for Logarithms, & an application to the advancement of Navigation.* <note>original French: "De la Chainette..." The "chainette" or catenary is the curve a hanging chain assumes under its own weight. Galileo mistakenly thought it was a parabola; Leibniz was among the first to provide the correct mathematical description using his new calculus.</note>
Journal of Scholars of March 31, 1692.

### XLIII. *

*On a Line formed from an infinite number of lines drawn in order intersecting among themselves, and tangent to them all; and on a new use of the Analysis of Infinities in that matter, by Author O. V. E.* <note>original Latin: "De Linea ex Lineis numero infinitis... Auth. O. V. E." This describes the geometric concept of an "envelope"—a curve that is tangent to a whole family of other lines or curves. "O.V.E." is a pseudonym Leibniz often used, standing for *Omnia Vincit Evergetes*.</note>
Leipzig Journal. April 1692. page 168.

Mr. Leibniz had already pointed out previously to Abbé Nicaise what he thought about Descartes; he discussed it at greater length with Mr. Christian Thomasius <note>A significant German jurist and philosopher (1655–1728) who helped bridge the gap between late scholasticism and the Enlightenment.</note>, who inserted into his book titled *History of Wisdom and Folly* <note>original Latin: *Historia Sapientiæ & Stultitiæ*.</note> what Mr. Leibniz had communicated to him concerning Descartes.

->### LXII. <-

*Diplomatic Code of the Law of Nations, in which are contained authentic tables of public records, mostly unpublished or selected, which G. G. L. edited from manuscripts, especially from the codices of the Augustan Library of Wolfenbüttel, and monuments from Royal and other archives, and finally from his own collections. Hanover, printed at the expense of Samuel Ammon, 1693, in folio.* <note>This "Codex Juris Gentium Diplomaticus" is one of Leibniz's most important historical and legal works, establishing a documentary basis for international law.</note>

This beautiful collection begins in the year 1096 and ends in 1499. All the pieces it contains are arranged in chronological order. He included a preface of good taste and great sense at the beginning. He later published a supplement to this collection. One may consult the Leipzig Journal, Year 1693, page 370, and Mr. Fabricius <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a famed German bibliographer.</note>, *History of his own Library* <note>original Latin: *Historia Biblioth. Propr.*</note>, Part 2, page 313, etc. We have also spoken at length regarding this work.

On the first correction of Philosophy, and on the notion of Substance.* <note>original Latin: *De prima Philosophiæ emendatione, & de notione Substantiæ.* This is a pivotal metaphysical text where Leibniz attempts to clarify the nature of reality and "substance" as an active force.</note>

*G. G. L. <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.</note> A new application and use of the Differential Calculus, for the manifold construction of Lines from a given condition of Tangents.* <note>original Latin: "Nova Calculi Differentialis applicatio, & usus, ad multiplicem Linearum Constructionem ex data Tangentium conditione." This work further develops Leibniz's methods for determining the shape of a curve based on the properties of its tangents.</note>

Leipzig Journal. Year 1694. page 311.

->### LXV. <-

*Letter on a Way to Perfect Medicine.*

*Journal des Savans* <note>The earliest academic journal published in Europe, based in France.</note> Year 1694, July 16th. This method, as Mr. Leibniz understands it here, would be to add each year to the Annual Lists of Baptisms & Deaths, a History of the constitution of the Air, of the Seasons, of the Diseases that have reigned among Animals, and of those that have been prevalent among Men, etc. This would follow roughly the plan of Ramazzini <note>Bernardino Ramazzini (1633–1714), an Italian physician known as the father of occupational medicine.</note>, which could easily be improved upon by having it done by public order, by skilled people, and by making it more general and extensive. Then, every year, a succinct Collection of this kind of Observations would be drawn up, which could only become of great use over time. All of this is very judicious: but, as Mr. Leibniz said himself, it is a truth as certain as it is deplorable, that the care of the Soul and the Body are the first things to which one should think, and the last to which one actually thinks.

This concerns a curve where a body moves such that its distance from a fixed point changes uniformly over time. "Osculations" refers to the "kissing" or contact between curves, specifically circles of curvature.</note>

Leipzig Journal. Year 1695. page 145.
Mr. Leibniz was persuaded that there is always the same amount of **Force** <note>Leibniz argued for the conservation of "living force" ($mv^2$), rather than the conservation of "quantity of motion" ($mv$).</note> found in Nature, and not the same amount of **Movement**, as Descartes believed. ### CXLIX.

G. G. L. *Inquiry into the Origin of the Franks.* <note>original: "De Origine Francorum Disquisitio." G.G.L. stands for Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. The Franks were the Germanic tribes whose expansion led to the formation of France and Germany.</note> Hannover 1715 in 12mo.

He first composed this small work in Latin, which we mentioned in his *Life*, and later provided an excellent French translation of it, which is included in the *Collection of Various Pieces on Philosophy, etc.* gathered by Mr. Des Maizeaux. The Latin original, published for the second time in Frankfurt in 1720 and expanded with a response to objections from several learned men, appeared as a supplement to the folio volume by Mr. Johann Georg von Eckhart, entitled *Laws of the Franks and the Ripuarians*. <note>original: "Leges Francorum & Ripuariorum." ->151.<-

*History of Bileam.* <note>original: "Histoire de Bileam." Bileam is the Hebrew form of the name more commonly known in English as Balaam.</note>

A theological pamphlet containing 19 pages in a small duodecimo <term>duodecimo: A book size where each sheet is folded into twelve leaves (12mo), creating a small, portable volume.</term> format, without the name of the author, printer, or place of printing, and without a date. Not knowing the time when it appeared, I place it here to conclude the list of works published by Mr. Leibniz during his lifetime. It concerns the *History of Balaam* (a Prophet or Diviner from the city of Pethor on the Euphrates) recorded in Holy Scripture in the Book of Numbers, Chapters 22, 23, 24, etc. Mr. Leibniz titled it the *History of Bileam*, reading the Hebrew word according to the tradition of the Masoretes. <note>The Masoretes were Jewish scholars between the 6th and 10th centuries who standardized the pronunciation and vocalization of the Hebrew Bible.</note> However, the difficulty does not lie in how the name of Balaam is read—that matters little—but rather in the explanation of the history itself, which divides all commentators of Scripture, both ancient and modern. The question is asked whether what Moses <note>In the 18th century, Moses was traditionally credited as the author of the Book of Numbers.</note> relates of Balaam, and especially of his dialogue with the female donkey, actually happened literally as the text seems to indicate, or if it is an allegory, a vision, or a dream. Mr. Leibniz, without entering into the discussion of these two opinions, embraces the latter interpretation and believes there is nothing in the words of the text contrary to it. <note>By interpreting the talking donkey as a prophetic vision or dream, Leibniz sought to reconcile the biblical narrative with a more rationalist philosophical framework.</note>

# P R E F A C E.

### *By Mr. Leibniz.*

It has been seen at all times that the common run of men has placed devotion in formalities; **solid piety**, <note>original: "la solide pieté"</note> that is to say, enlightenment and virtue, has never been the shared lot of the many. One must not be at all surprised by this; nothing is so consistent with human weakness. We are struck by the external, while the internal requires a deliberation of which few people render themselves capable. As true piety consists in sentiments and in practice, *the formalities of devotion* imitate it, and are of two kinds; some correspond to *ceremonies of practice*, and others to *formulas of belief*. <term>Ceremonies</term> <note>Leibniz refers here to religious rituals and outward acts of worship.</note> resemble virtuous actions, and <term>formulas</term> <note>These are "confessions of faith" or "creeds"—the specific wording of a religious doctrine.</note> are like shadows of the Truth, and approach more or less the pure light. All these formalities would be laudable, if those who invented them had made them suitable to maintain and to express that which they imitate; if the reli-

-> P R E F A C E. <-

[without] any reflection on the strange consequences of this argument, which would prove too much: since it would prove (for example) that one should take a pleasant drink, even if one knew it was poisoned. For by the same reason (if it were valid) I could say: if it is written in the Archives of the Fates <note>original: "Archives des Parques," referring to the personifications of destiny in Roman mythology who spin and cut the thread of life</note>, that the poison will kill me now, or will do me harm, that will happen even if I were not to take this drink; and if it is not written, it will not happen, even though I were to take this same drink; and consequently I will be able to follow my inclination to take what is agreeable with impunity, however pernicious it may be, which contains a manifest absurdity. It is that it is false that the event happens regardless of what one does; it will happen because one does what leads to it: and if the event is written, the cause that will make it happen is written also. XXVIII
-># P R E F A C E.<-

...will. The **Author** of this **Discourse** believes he has provided proof of this here by the diligence he has applied to this subject. —truths, but particularly (when it is compared with Faith) of those which the human mind can reach naturally without being aided by the lights of Faith. This definition of Reason (that is to say, of *right and true Reason* <note>Leibniz is invoking the classical concept of *recta ratio*, which views reason not as a subjective opinion, but as an objective, logical standard of truth.</note>) has surprised some people accustomed to railing against Reason when taken in a vague sense. They replied to me that they had never heard this meaning given to it; this is because they had never conferred with people who explained themselves clearly on these matters. They admitted to me, however, that one could not blame Reason when taken in the sense I gave it. It is in this same sense that Reason is sometimes opposed to Experience. Reason, consisting in the linking of truths, has the right to also link those that experience has furnished it, in order to draw mixed conclusions: but pure and naked Reason, distinguished from experience, deals only with truths independent of the Senses. And one can compare Faith with Experience, since Faith (regarding the motives that verify it) depends on the experience of those who saw the miracles upon which revelation is founded, and on the trustworthy Tradition which has passed them down to us, whether by the Scriptures or by the report of those who preserved them. It is much like how we base ourselves on the experience of those who have seen China, and on the credibility of their report, when we place faith in the wonders told to us about that distant country <note>In the 17th century, China was a popular example among philosophers to illustrate "moral certainty"—things we believe to be true based on the reliable testimony of others rather than our own direct observation.</note>; saving for elsewhere the discussion of the internal movement of the Holy Spirit, which takes hold of souls, persuades them, and leads them to the good—that is, to faith and to charity—without always needing external motives.

It is therefore true that it is not without reason that God has given them, for he chooses nothing by caprice, and as if by chance, or through pure indifference; but the general reasons of goodness and order which moved him to do so can be outweighed in certain cases by greater reasons of a superior order.

### OF FAITH AND REASON.

carefully; and all that is said against Reason only strikes at a pretended Reason, corrupted and deceived by false appearances. It is the same with the notions of the justice and the goodness of God. People sometimes speak of them as if we had no idea or definition of them. But in that case, we would have no foundation for attributing these attributes to Him, or for praising Him for them. His goodness and His justice, as well as His wisdom, differ from ours only because they are infinitely more perfect. Thus, simple notions, necessary truths, and the demonstrative consequences of **Philosophy** cannot be contrary to **Revelation**. And when certain philosophical maxims are rejected in **Theology**, it is because they are held to be only of a physical or moral necessity <note>Leibniz distinguishes between "logical necessity" (things that cannot be otherwise, like 2+2=4) and "physical necessity" (laws of nature like gravity, which God could theoretically suspend to perform a miracle).</note>, which speaks only of what ordinarily takes place, and is consequently founded on appearances, but which may fail if God sees fit.

And I find that Mr. Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a famous skeptic and author. It is also not possible for us to *prove* **Mysteries** by **Reason**: for everything that can be proved *from the start* <note>original: "à priori"; referring to reasoning derived from theoretical principles or causes rather than observation.</note>, or by pure reason, can be understood. after having placed faith in the Mysteries based on the proofs of the truth of Religion (which are called <term>motifs of credibility</term> <note>Arguments or evidence that make a religious claim seem reasonable or worthy of belief, even if they don't provide a mathematical proof.</note>), it is necessary to be able to uphold them against objections. Without this, we would have no foundation for believing them; for anything that can be refuted in a solid and demonstrative manner cannot fail to be false. Furthermore, the proofs of the truth of Religion—which can only provide <term>moral certainty</term> <note>A high degree of probability that is sufficient for human action and belief, distinct from the "absolute" certainty of logic or math.</note>—would be balanced and even overcome by objections that would provide <term>absolute certainty</term>, if those objections were convincing and entirely demonstrative. This small point would be enough to resolve the difficulties regarding the use of Reason and Philosophy in relation to Religion, if we were not so often dealing with prejudiced individuals. But since the matter is important and has been greatly muddled, it will be appropriate to enter into greater detail.

6. *The Question of the Conformity of Faith with Reason has always been a great Problem.* In the early Church, the most learned Christian authors adapted the thoughts of the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato, whose focus on the soul and an ideal, non-physical world appealed to early Christian thinkers.</note>, which suited them best and were the most fashionable at the time. Gradually, Aristotle <note>An ancient Greek philosopher whose work focused on logic, categorization, and the natural world; his methods became the standard for late medieval thought.</note> took the place of Plato when the taste for "Systems" began to prevail, and when Theology itself became more *Systematic* through the decisions of the General Councils, which provided precise and positive Formularies <note>Official statements of belief or doctrine.</note>. Saint Augustine, Boethius, and Cassiodorus in the West, and St. John of Damascus in the East, contributed the most to reducing Theology to the form of a science—not to mention Bede, Alcuin, St. Anselm, and several other theologians well-versed in Philosophy. Finally, the Scholastics <note>Medieval scholars who taught in European universities (the "Schools") and sought to reconcile Christian doctrine with Aristotelian logic.</note> arrived; as the leisure of the cloisters gave free rein to speculation—aided by the Philosophy of Aristotle translated from Arabic—a composite of Theology and Philosophy was eventually formed, in

[excel]lence, and who appeared to have entered best into the sense of Aristotle among those of his nation. <note>Leibniz refers to Averroës (Ibn Rushd), a medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly influential and controversial in Europe.</note> This Commentator, pushing further what certain Greek interpreters had already taught, claimed that according to Aristotle, and even according to Reason (which was then taken for almost the same thing), the immortality of the Soul could not subsist. Here is his reasoning: The human race is eternal according to Aristotle; therefore, if individual souls do not perish, one must accept <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>The migration of a soul from one body into another after death; reincarnation.</note>, which was rejected by this Philosopher. Or, if there are always new souls, one must admit the infinity of these souls preserved from all eternity; but an <term>actual infinite</term> <note>A completed, infinite total of objects existing at once, which many medieval philosophers deemed logically impossible.</note> is impossible according to the doctrine of this same Aristotle. Therefore, one must conclude that Souls—that is to say, the forms of organic bodies—must perish with those bodies; or at least the <term>passive intellect</term> <note>In Aristotelian thought, the part of the mind that receives sensory information and is tied to the physical body.</note> belonging specifically to each individual. So that there will only remain the <term>active intellect</term> <note>The part of the mind that processes abstract truths, which Averroës argued was a single, universal entity shared by all humans rather than a personal trait.</note>, common to all men, which Aristotle said comes from without, and which must work wherever the organs are prepared for it; just as the wind produces a kind of music when it is pushed into well-adjusted organ pipes.

8. There was nothing weaker than this supposed demonstration; it is not found that Aristotle effectively refuted Metempsychosis, nor that he proved the eternity of the human race; and after all, it is very false that an actual infinite is impossible. However, this demonstration passed for invincible among the <term>Aristotelians</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, and led them to believe that there was a certain <term>sublunary Intelligence</term> <note>A spiritual being or mind existing below the level of the moon (the earthly realm) that governs human thought.</note>, whose participation created our active intellect. But others, less attached to Aristotle, went as far as a universal soul which was the Ocean of all particular souls, and believed this universal soul alone capable of subsisting, while particular souls are born and perish.

**23.** The distinction usually made between *what is above Reason* and *what is against Reason* agrees well enough with the distinction just made between the two kinds of necessity. For what is against Reason is against absolutely certain and indispensable truths; and what is above Reason is contrary only to what we are accustomed to experience or understand. This is why I am surprised that there are men of wit who combat this distinction, and that Mr. Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a hugely influential French philosopher and skeptic known for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*. But a truth can never be against Reason; and far from a dogma attacked and refuted by Reason being incomprehensible, one might say that nothing is easier to understand, nor more manifest, than its absurdity. # DISCOURSE ON THE CONFORMITY OF FAITH WITH REASON
<meta>catchword: to have</meta>

...to have sufficient reasons to prove it; otherwise two contradictories would be true at the same time. One must always yield to demonstrations, whether they are proposed to affirm [a point] or whether they are put forward in the form of objections. And it is unjust and useless to want to weaken the proofs of opponents under the pretext that they are merely objections; since the opponent has the same right, and can reverse the labels, honoring his arguments with the name of **proofs**, and demeaning ours with the disparaging name of **objections**.

26. It is another question whether we are always obliged to examine the objections that can be made against us, and to maintain some doubt about our opinion—or what is called the *fear of the opposite* <note>original: "Formidinem oppositi". In scholastic philosophy, this refers to the uncertainty or anxiety that the contrary of one's belief might actually be true.</note>—until that examination has been conducted. I would venture to say no, for otherwise one would never reach certainty, and our conclusion would always be provisional. I believe that skilled geometricians will hardly trouble themselves with the objections of Joseph Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609) was a great scholar who famously, and incorrectly, claimed to have solved the mathematical problem of "squaring the circle."</note> against Archimedes, or those of Mr. Hobbes <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the English philosopher, who had famous and often misguided disputes with the leading mathematicians of his day regarding geometry.</note> against Euclid; but this is because they are very sure of the demonstrations they have understood. Nevertheless, it is sometimes good to have the courtesy to examine certain objections; for besides the fact that this can serve to lead people out of their error, it may happen that we ourselves profit from it; for specious <term>Paralogisms</term> <note>A paralogism is a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning, specifically one where the person making the argument is unaware of its flaw.</note> often contain some useful insight and provide an occasion to resolve some significant difficulties. It seems here that, according to Mr. Bayle, rendering a reason <note>providing a logical proof of why something is true</note> is less than answering objections, since he threatens the person who would undertake the first with the obligation of going as far as the second. But it is quite the opposite: a respondent <term>respondens: the student or scholar defending a thesis in a formal academic debate</term> is not at all obliged to render a reason for his thesis, but he is obliged to satisfy the arguments of an opponent. A defendant in a court of Justice is not obliged (ordinarily) to prove his right, or to put forward the title of his possession; but he is obliged to answer the reasons of the plaintiff. And I have wondered a hundred times that an Author as exact and as penetrating as Mr. Bayle so often mixes things here where there is as much difference as there is between these three acts of Reason: understanding, proving, and answering objections; as if when it comes to the use of Reason in Theology, one were worth as much as the other. This is how he says in his *Posthumous Conversations* <note>original: *Entretiens posthumes*</note> p. 73: *There is no principle that Mr. Bayle has more often instilled than this one: that the incomprehensibility of a Dogma and the insolubility of the objections that combat it, is not a legitimate reason to reject it.* Incomprehensibility is one thing, but the same is not true for "insolubility." And it is indeed the same as if one said that an invincible reason against a thesis is not a legitimate reason to reject it. For what other legitimate reason for rejecting an opinion can one find, if an invincible contrary argument is not one? And what means will one have after that to demonstrate the falsehood and even the absurdity of any opinion?

It is also useful to observe that he who proves a thing *a priori* <note>original: "à priori"; a Latin term meaning reasoning from causes to effects, or from theoretical principles rather than experience.</note>, provides a reason for it through its efficient cause <term>efficient cause: the primary source or agent that brings something into being.</term>, and whoever can provide such reasons in an exact and sufficient manner is also in a position to understand the thing. This is why the Scholastic theologians <note>Scholasticism was a medieval school of philosophy that used logic and reason to resolve contradictions in Christian doctrine.</note> had already blamed Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher who created a logical "Art" intended to prove Christian truths to non-believers.</note> for having undertaken to demonstrate the Trinity through Philosophy. One will therefore blame those who wish to provide a reason for this Mystery and make it comprehensible, but one will praise those who work to sustain it against the objections of adversaries.

60. I have already said that Theologians ordinarily distinguish between what is *above Reason* and what is *against Reason*. They categorize as *above Reason* that which one cannot understand, and for which one cannot provide a reason. But *against Reason* will be any sentiment that is contested by invincible reasons, or else whose contradictory can be proved in an exact and solid manner. They thus admit that Mysteries are above Reason, but they do not at all grant that they are contrary to it. The English Author of an ingenious but disapproved Book, titled *Christianity Not Mysterious* <note>Written by John Toland in 1696, this controversial work argued that nothing in the Gospel is contrary to reason nor above it, and that mysteries are merely things not yet explained.</note>, wished to combat this distinction, but it does not appear to me that he has made any dent in it. Mr. Bayle also is not entirely satisfied with this received distinction. Here is what he says about it (Volume 3 of the *Reply to the Questions of a Provincial*, chapter 158), first (page 998): He distinguishes with Mr. Saurin <note>Élie Saurin (1639–1703), a French Protestant minister in exile who debated Pierre Bayle on the nature of reason and faith.</note> between these two theses: one, *all the dogmas of Christianity agree with Reason*; the other, *Rea-*

<meta>catchword: fen-</meta>

*Human Reason knows that they agree with Reason.* He admits the first, and denies the second. I am of the same opinion, if by saying that a *Dogma agrees with Reason*, one means that it is possible to provide a reason for it, or to explain the *how* of it through Reason; for God could undoubtedly do so, and we cannot. But I believe one must affirm both theses if, by *knowing that a dogma agrees with Reason*, one means that we can show when necessary that there is no contradiction between this Dogma and Reason, by repelling the objections of those who claim that this Dogma is an absurdity.

61. Mr. Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a hugely influential French philosopher and skeptic. His *Historical and Critical Dictionary* often highlighted the apparent contradictions between religious faith and logical reason.</note> explains himself here in a manner that is not at all satisfying. He recognizes very well that our Mysteries are conformable to the supreme and universal Reason which is in the divine Understanding, or to Reason in general; however, he denies that they appear conformable to that portion of Reason which man uses to judge things. But since this portion of Reason that we possess is a gift from God, and consists in the natural light <term>natural light: the innate human capacity for logic and basic truths, which Enlightenment thinkers believed was granted to all humans by God or nature.</term> that remains with us in the midst of corruption; this portion is in conformity with the whole, and it differs from that which is in God only as a drop of water differs from the Ocean, or rather as the finite from the infinite. Thus, Mysteries may surpass it, but they could not be contrary to it. One cannot be contrary to a part without being contrary in that respect to the whole. That which contradicts a proposition of Euclid is contrary to the *Elements* of Euclid <note>Euclid’s *Elements* was the standard textbook for geometry and logic for over 2,000 years; Leibniz uses it here as the ultimate example of a consistent, logical system where every part must agree with the whole.</note>. That which in us is contrary to Mysteries is not Reason, nor the natural light, nor the linking of truths; it is corruption, it is error or prejudice, it is darkness.

...above **Reason**, it is usually said, but they are not contrary to **Reason**. I believe that one does not give the same meaning to the word **Reason** in the first part of this Axiom as in the second; and that one understands in the first part human **Reason**, or **Reason** in the concrete <note>original: "in concreto"; referring to reason as it is applied by humans in specific instances</note>, and in the second part **Reason** in general, or **Reason** in the abstract <note>original: "in abstracto"; referring to the pure, ideal principles of logic and truth</note>. For, assuming that one always means **Reason** in general, or **Supreme Reason**, the **Universal Reason** which is in God, it is equally true that the **Evangelical Mysteries** are not at all above **Reason**, and that they are not against **Reason**. But if one understands human **Reason** in both parts of the Axiom, I do not see much solidity in the distinction: for the most **Orthodox** <note>Standard or traditional believers of the time.</note> admit that we do not know the conformity of our **Mysteries** with the maxims of **Philosophy**. It seems to us, then, that they are not conformable to our **Reason**. Now, that which seems to us not to be conformable to our **Reason** seems contrary to our **Reason**: just as that which does not seem conformable to the truth seems contrary to the truth: and so, why should one not say equally both that the **Mysteries** are against our weak **Reason**, and that they are above our weak **Reason**? I answer, as I have already done, that **Reason** here is the chain of truths <note>The logical sequence where one truth follows from another through proof.</note> that we know by the natural light <note>The innate human capacity for logic and understanding, gifted by God.</note>, and in this sense the accepted axiom is true without any ambiguity. The **Mysteries** surpass our **Reason**, for they contain truths that are not included in this chain; but they are not at all contrary to our **Reason**, and do not contradict any of the truths to which this chain can lead us. It is therefore not a question here of the **Universal Reason** which is in God, but of our own. As for the question of whether we know the conformity of the **Mysteries** with our **Reason**, I reply that at the very least we never know that there...

64. Mr. Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a French philosopher known for his influential "Historical and Critical Dictionary" and his skeptical views on the relationship between faith and reason.</note> makes another ingenious objection, which he draws from the example of the sense of sight. *When a square tower (he says) appears round to us from a distance, not only do our eyes testify very clearly that they perceive nothing square in this tower, but also that they discover there a round figure, incompatible with the square figure. One can therefore say that the truth, which is the square figure, is not only above, but even against the testimony of our weak sight.* It must be admitted that this remark is true; and although it is true that the appearance of roundness comes from the mere absence of the appearance of the angles which distance causes to disappear, it remains true nonetheless that the round and the square are opposite things. I reply, then, to this instance, that the representation of the senses, even when they do all that depends on them, is often contrary to truth; but it is not the same with the faculty of reasoning, when it does its duty, since exact reasoning is nothing other than a **chain of truths**. And as for the sense of sight in particular, it is good to consider that there are still other false appearances which do not come at all from the weakness of our *eyes*, nor from what disappears through distance; but from the nature of vision itself, however perfect it may be. It is thus, for example, that the circle seen from the side is changed into that species of oval which is called an **Ellipse** among **Geometricians** <note>mathematicians who study the properties of space and shapes</note>, and

*...that we understand nothing else than that we know it to be incomprehensible by its nature.*

69. This passage by Mr. Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher famous for "I think, therefore I am."</note>, followed by his disciples (who rarely take it upon themselves to doubt what he puts forward), has always seemed strange to me. Not contenting himself with saying that, for his part, he sees no way to reconcile the two <term>dogmas</term> <note>The two specific religious doctrines here are human free will and God's all-knowing planning (providence).</note>, he places the entire human race, and even all rational creatures, in the same position. However, could he be unaware that it is impossible for there to be an invincible objection against the truth? For such an objection could only be a necessary chain of other truths, the result of which would be contrary to the truth one is defending; consequently, there would be a contradiction between truths, which is the ultimate absurdity. Furthermore, although our mind is finite and cannot encompass the infinite, it nonetheless possesses demonstrations regarding the infinite, the strength or weakness of which it understands; why, then, should it not understand the strength of the objections? And since the power and wisdom of God are infinite and encompass everything, there is no longer any reason to doubt their extent. Moreover, Mr. Descartes demands a freedom that is not needed, by wishing for the actions of human will to be entirely <term>indeterminate</term> <note>Descartes argued that for a choice to be truly free, it must not be strictly determined by prior causes.</note>, which never happens. Finally, Mr. Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a skeptical philosopher whose "Historical and Critical Dictionary" Leibniz is largely responding to in this work.</note> himself maintains that this experience or inner feeling of our independence, upon which Mr. Descartes builds the proof of our freedom, does not prove it at all; for just because we do not perceive the causes upon which we depend, it does not follow that we are independent. But that is something we shall speak of in its proper place.

...minate to infinity, which he nevertheless recognizes as true. Arriaga <note>Rodrigo de Arriaga (1592–1667) was a Spanish Jesuit philosopher known for his work on logic and physics.</note> and other Scholastics <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Followers of a medieval school of philosophy that used Aristotelian logic to resolve theological questions.</note> make nearly the same admission; but if they took the trouble to give their objections the proper logical form, they would see that there are errors in the conclusion, and sometimes false assumptions that create confusion. 

Here is an example: A clever man once presented me with this objection: Let a straight line BA be cut into two equal parts at point C, and the part CA into two at point D, and the part DA into two at point E, and so on to infinity. All these halves—BC, CD, DE, etc.—together make up the whole line BA. Therefore, there must be a "last half," since the straight line BA ends at point A. But this "last half" is absurd: for since it is a line, it could still be cut in two. Therefore, the idea of division to infinity cannot be admitted. 

But I pointed out to him that one has no right to infer that there must be a "last point" A <note>In this context, Leibniz is arguing against the idea of a final, indivisible segment of a line.</note>, for this final point belongs to all the halves on its side. My friend recognized this himself when he tried to prove his conclusion through a formal argument: on the contrary, by the very fact that the division goes on to infinity, there is no "last half" at all. And although the straight line AB is finite, it does not follow that the process of dividing it has a final term. 

We find ourselves similarly entangled in series of numbers that go to infinity. We imagine a "last term," an "infinite number," or an "infinitely small" quantity, but all of these are merely fictions. Every number is finite and assignable; every line is the same. The "infinite" or "infinitely small" only signify magnitudes that one can take as large or as small as one wishes, in order to show that an error is less than any specified amount—which is to say, that there is no error at all. Alternatively, one understands the "infinitely small" as the state of vanishing <note>original: "évanouïffement"; This refers to the concept of a mathematical limit, where a value approaches zero.</note>

The detail we have entered into here will serve as an answer to several other arguments on this subject found scattered throughout the works of Mr. Bayle, such as when he says in his *Response to the Questions of a Provincial*, chapter 133 (volume 3, page 685): *To prove that one has reconciled Reason and Religion, one must show not only that one has philosophical maxims which are favorable to our faith, but also that the specific maxims which are raised against us as not conforming to our Catechism <note>In this context, the "Catechism" refers to the established doctrines or summaries of religious belief</note> are indeed conforming to it in a manner that is distinctly conceived.* I do not see that all this is needed, unless one intends to push the reasoning as far as the *how* of the Mystery. When one is satisfied with upholding its truth without getting involved in wanting to make it understood, one has no need to resort to philosophical maxims, general or specific, for proof; and when another person opposes us with certain philosophical maxims, it is not for us to prove in a clear and distinct manner that these maxims are in conformity with our dogma, but it is up to our opponent to prove that they are contrary to it.

He further adds: *If we must offer a reply and a rejoinder <note>original: "repliquer & dupliquer," technical terms for the successive rounds of a formal academic or legal debate</note>, we must never fall behind, nor claim that we have achieved our goal, as long as our opponent replies to us with things as evident as our reasons could be.* But it is not the task of the <term>respondent</term> <note>The "soutenant" or defender in a debate, who only needs to show that the opponent's attacks are not decisive</note> to provide reasons; it is enough for him to answer those of his opponent.

79. The Author [Bayle] finally concludes: *If one claimed that, when making an evident objection, one must be satisfied with an answer that we can only give as a possible thing, and that we do not understand, it would be unjust.* He repeats this in the *Posthumous Dialogues* against <term>Mr. Jaquelot</term> <note>Isaac Jaquelot (1647–1708), a French Protestant theologian who, like Leibniz, attempted to defend the compatibility of reason and faith against Bayle's skepticism</note>, page 69. I do not share this sentiment. If the objection were perfectly evident, it would be victorious, and the Thesis would be destroyed. But when the objection is founded only on appearances, or on cases that happen most often, and when the person making it wants to draw a universal and certain conclusion from it, the one who upholds the Mystery can respond with the instance of a simple possibility. Such an instance is enough to show that what the opponent wanted to infer from the premises is neither certain nor general; and it is enough for the one who fights for the Mystery to maintain that it is possible, without needing to maintain that it is <term>plausible</term> <note>original: "vraisemblable," meaning likely or having the appearance of truth</note>. For, as I have often said, it is agreed that Mysteries are against appearances. The one who defends the Mystery would not even need to provide such an instance, and if he does so, one might say it is a <term>work of supererogation</term> <note>An action that goes beyond what is required by duty; in this context, Leibniz means the defender is doing more than the rules of logic strictly require of them</note>, or that it is a means of better confounding the opponent.

## OF FAITH WITH REASON
<page-num>65</page-num>

Bayle (it is said, p. 36, 37) constantly asserts in his *Dictionary* <note>Pierre Bayle’s *Dictionnaire Historique et Critique*, a massive and influential work of the late 17th century that used skeptical arguments to challenge religious and philosophical certainties</note>, whenever the subject allows, that our *Reason* is more capable of *refuting* and *destroying* than of *proving* and *building*; that there is almost no *Philosophical* or *Theological* matter upon which it does not raise very great difficulties; so that if one wanted to follow it with a spirit of dispute, as far as it can go, one would often find oneself reduced to an unfortunate impasse; finally, that there are doctrines which are certainly true, which it combats with insoluble objections. I believe that what is said here to blame Reason is to its advantage. When it destroys some <term>Thesis</term> <note>A formal proposition or statement put forward to be maintained or proved</note>, it builds up the opposite Thesis. And when it seems to destroy two opposite Theses at the same time, it is then that it promises us something profound, provided that we follow it as far as it *can go*, not with a spirit of dispute, but with an ardent desire to seek and disentangle the truth, which will always be rewarded by some considerable success.

81. Mr. Bayle continues: *that one must then mock these objections by recognizing the narrow limits of the human mind*. And I, I believe that far from that, one must recognize in them signs of the strength of the human mind, which allows it to penetrate into the interior of things. These are new openings, and so to speak, rays of the dawn of day, which promise us a greater light; I mean this in matters of Philosophy or <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>The branch of philosophy that attempts to prove God's existence and attributes through reason and observation of nature, without relying on supernatural revelation</note>: but when these objections are made against <term>Revealed Faith</term> <note>Truths considered to be revealed directly by God (such as through scripture) which may exceed the grasp of human reason</note>, it is enough that one can repel them, provided that one does so with a spirit of submission and zeal, with the intent to maintain and exalt the glory of God. And when one succeeds in this regard concerning His justice, one will be equally struck by His grandeur and charmed by His goodness, which will appear through the clouds of a...

82. *Thus* (to continue with Mr. Bayle) *one will oblige Reason to lay down its arms, and to surrender itself under the obedience of Faith, which it can and must do by virtue of some of its most incontestable maxims; and thus, in renouncing some of its other maxims, it nonetheless continues to act according to what it is, that is to say, as Reason.* But it must be known that the maxims of Reason which must be renounced in this case are only those that make us judge based on appearances, or according to the ordinary course of things: something which Reason commands us to do even in Philosophical matters when there are invincible proofs to the contrary. # *PART ONE.*

After having established the rights of Faith and Reason in a manner that makes Reason serve Faith, far from being contrary to it, we shall see how they exercise these rights to maintain and reconcile together what natural light <term>natural light: The human capacity for logic and reason, independent of divine revelation.</term> and revealed light <term>revealed light: Truths communicated directly by God, such as those found in the Bible.</term> teach us of God and man in relation to evil. One may distinguish the *Difficulties* into two *Classes*. Some arise from the freedom of Man, which seems incompatible with the divine nature; and yet, freedom is judged necessary so that Man may be judged guilty and punishable. The others concern the conduct of God, which seems to make him take too much of a part in the existence of evil,

even if Man were free and played his part in it. And this conduct seems contrary to divine goodness, holiness, and justice: since God concurs <term>concurs: From the theological concept of "divine concurrence," the idea that God’s power is the immediate cause of every action in the universe, working alongside the will of his creatures.</term> with evil, both Physical and Moral; and he concurs with both in a moral way, as well as in a physical way, and it seems that these evils are seen in the order of nature, as well as in the order of grace; and in the future and eternal life, as much as and even more than in this fleeting life.

2. To represent these difficulties in brief, it must be noted that freedom is opposed (in appearance) by determination or by certainty of any kind; and yet the common dogma of our Philosophers holds that the truth of **future contingents** <term>future contingents: Events that may or may not happen in the future, which are not logically necessary (like "2+2=4") but are still true or false in God's eyes before they happen.</term> is determined. The foreknowledge of God also makes the whole future certain and determined; but his providence and his preordination, upon which foreknowledge itself seems founded, does much more: for God is not like a Man, who can look upon events with indifference, and who can suspend his judgment; since nothing exists except following the decrees of his will and by the action of his power. And even if one were to set aside the concurrence of God, everything is perfectly linked in the order of things: since nothing could happen without there being a cause disposed as is necessary to produce the effect: which occurs no less in voluntary actions than in all others. After which it appears that man is forced to do the good and the evil he does; and consequently that he deserves neither reward nor punishment, which destroys the **Morality** of actions, and shocks all divine and human justice.

3. But even if one granted to Man this liberty of which he boasts to his own detriment; the conduct of God would still provide matter for criticism,

It is objected that all reality, and what is called the **substance of the act**, even in sin, is a production of God, since all creatures and all their actions derive from him whatever reality they possess; from which one would wish to infer not only that he is the <term>Physical cause: The immediate, natural power that brings an effect into being.</term> **Physical cause** of sin, but also that he is its **Moral cause**, since he acts very freely, and does nothing without a perfect knowledge of the thing and the consequences it may have. And it is not enough to say that God has made it a law for himself to **concur** <note>concur: To work together with the will of a creature to produce an action.</note> with the wills or revolutions <note>original: "révolutions"; here meaning the internal changes or movements of the soul.</note> of Man, whether in the common opinion or in the **System of occasional causes** <term>System of occasional causes: A philosophical theory (notably by Malebranche) suggesting that created things do not truly act on each other, but provide "occasions" for God to act.</term>; for besides the fact that one would find it strange that he made such a law, whose consequences he was not ignorant of, the principal difficulty is that it seems the evil will itself could not exist without a concurrence, and even without some **predetermination** on his part that contributes to bringing this will into being in Man, or in some other rational creature: for an action, by virtue of being evil, is no less dependent on God: from which one will finally want to conclude that God does everything indifferently, both good and evil: unless one wishes to say, with the **Manichaeans**, that there are two principles, one good and the other evil. Furthermore, following the common sentiment of Theologians and Philosophers, conservation being a **continual creation**, it will be said that Man is continually created, corrupted, and sinning. Moreover, there are modern **Cartesians** who claim that God is the sole actor, of whom creatures are but purely passive organs, and **Mr. Bayle** relies not a little upon this.

Man is exposed to a temptation to which it is known he will succumb, and that thereby he will be the cause of an infinity of dreadful evils; that by this fall the whole Human race will be infected and placed in a kind of necessity of sinning, which is called **original sin**; that the world will be placed thereby in a strange confusion; that by this means death and diseases will be introduced, with a thousand other misfortunes and miseries which ordinarily afflict the good and the bad; that wickedness will even reign, and that virtue will be oppressed here below; and that thus it will hardly appear at all that a **providence** governs things.

But it is much worse when one considers the life to come, since there will be only a small number of Men who will be saved, and all the others will perish eternally: besides the fact that these Men destined for salvation will have been removed from the <note>original: "maſſe corrompuë"; a reference to the Augustinian concept of *massa damnata*, the idea that all humanity is a "corrupt mass" deserving of punishment due to original sin.</note> **corrupted mass** by an **election** without reason; whether it is said that God, in choosing them, had regard for their future good actions, for their Faith or for their works, or whether it is claimed that he wished to give them these good qualities and these actions because he **predestined** them for salvation. > *Behold, how much more piercing is our weapon.* <note>original Latin: "Aspice, quàm mage sit nostrum penetrabile telum." A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, suggesting that the truth of the argument is more powerful than the objections raised against it.</note>

7. ***God is the first Reason of things:*** for those that are limited, like all that we see and experience, are <term>contingent: In philosophy, "contingent" refers to things that exist but do not have to exist by their own nature; they could have been different or not existed at all.</term>, and have nothing in themselves that makes their existence necessary; it being manifest that time, space, and matter, united and uniform in themselves, and indifferent to everything, could have received entirely different motions and figures, and in another order altogether. It is also necessary that this cause be intelligent: for this World that exists being contingent, and an infinity of other Worlds being equally possible and equally "claiming" existence, so to speak, as much as it does, the cause of the world must have had regard or relation to all these <term>possible Worlds: A central concept for Leibniz, suggesting that before creation, God’s mind contained an infinite number of ways the universe could have been designed.</term> in order to determine one. And it is the ***power*** of this substance that makes its will effective. Power leads to ***being***, wisdom or understanding to the ***true***, and the will to the ***good***. And this intelligent cause must be infinite in every way, and absolutely perfect in power, in wisdom, and in goodness, since it extends to everything...

8. Now this supreme wisdom, joined to a goodness that is no less infinite than it is, could not have failed to choose the best. For just as a lesser evil is a kind of good, so a lesser good is a kind of evil if it stands in the way of a greater good; and there would be something to correct in God's actions if there were a way to do better. And just as in mathematics, when there is no *maximum* <note>original Latin: "the greatest"</note> nor *minimum* <note>original Latin: "the least"</note>, nor anything distinguished at all, everything happens equally; or when that is not possible, nothing happens at all; one can say the same in the matter of perfect wisdom, which is no less regulated than mathematics: that if there were no best world (<note>original Latin: *optimum*</note>) among all possible worlds, God would have produced none. <insert>I call *World* the entire sequence and the entire collection of all existing things</insert>, so that no one might say that several worlds could exist at different times and in different places. For it would be necessary to count them all together as one world, or if you prefer, one Universe. And even if one were to fill all times and all places, it remains true that they could have been filled in an infinite number of ways, and that there is an infinity of possible worlds, from which God must have chosen the best, since he does nothing without acting according to supreme Reason.

which approaches pain, to show that there is something similar in intellectual pleasures. A little acidity, sharpness, or bitterness often pleases more than sugar; shadows enhance colors; and even a dissonance placed where it is needed gives relief to the harmony. We want to be frightened by tightrope dancers <note>original: "danseurs de corde"</note> who are on the point of falling, and we want Tragedies to make us almost weep. 13. But it will be said that evils are great and numerous in comparison to goods: one is mistaken. It is only a lack of attention that diminishes our goods, and it is necessary that this attention be given to us by some mixture of evils. If we were ordinarily sick and rarely in good health, we would marvelously feel this great good, and we would feel our evils less; but is it not better, nonetheless, for health to be common and sickness rare? Let us therefore supplement by our reflection what is lacking in our perception, in order to make the good of health more perceptible to us. If we had no knowledge of the future life <note>Referring to the afterlife or the immortality of the soul.</note>, I believe there would be few people who, at the moment of death, would not be content to take up life again on the condition of passing through the same value of goods and evils, provided above all that it were not of the same kind. One would be satisfied with variety, without demanding a better condition than that in which one had been.

15. Those who are of a mind to praise nature and fortune, and not to complain about them—even if they were not the most favored—seem to me preferable to others. For besides the fact that these complaints are ill-founded, it is, in effect, murmuring against the orders of **Providence**. One must not easily be among the number of the malcontents in the Republic where one lives, and one must not be so at all in the **City of God** <note>A reference to St. Augustine’s "De Civitate Dei," representing the spiritual community of the righteous under God's rule.</note>, where one can only be so with injustice. Books on human misery, such as that of **Pope Innocent III** <note>Referring to "De Miseria Condicionis Humanae" (On the Misery of the Human Condition), a 12th-century treatise emphasizing human frailty and sin.</note>, do not seem to me to be the most useful: one redoubles evils by giving them an attention that should be turned away from them, to be turned instead toward the goods which far outweigh them. I approve even less of books such as that by **Abbé Esprit** on the *falsity of human virtues*, of which an abridgment was recently given to us; such a book serves only to turn everything toward the bad side, and to make men such as it represents them.

21. One can take evil metaphysically, physically, and morally. **Metaphysical evil** consists in simple imperfection, **physical evil** in suffering, and **moral evil** in sin. Now, although physical evil and moral evil are not necessary, it is enough that, by virtue of the eternal truths, they are possible. And as this immense **Region** of truths contains all possibilities, there must be an infinity of possible Worlds, and evil enters into many of them, and even the best of all worlds contains it; this is what determined God to permit evil.

This will is called *antecedent* <term>Antecedent Will: In Leibniz's thought, this is God's initial desire for every individual good thing (like the happiness of every person) before considering how they all fit together.</term>, when it is detached and considers each good separately as a good. In this sense, one can say that God tends toward every good as a good—<note>original: "ad perfectionem simpliciter simplicem"</note> *toward perfection in its absolute simplicity*, to speak in the **Scholastic** <note>The Scholastics were medieval philosophers and theologians who used a highly structured, logical method of inquiry.</note> manner; and this is done by an antecedent will. He has a serious inclination to sanctify and to save all men, to exclude sin, and to prevent damnation. One can even say that this will is effective <note>original: "per se"</note> *by itself*—that is to say, in such a way that the effect would follow if there were not some stronger reason that prevented it; for this will does not go to the <note>original: "ad summum conatum"</note> *ultimate effort*, otherwise it would never fail to produce its full effect, God being the master of all things. Full and infallible success belongs only to the *consequent will* <term>Consequent Will: This is God’s final "resultant" will—the decision he makes after weighing all possible goods and evils against each other to create the best possible world.</term>, as it is called. It is this will which is "full," and in its regard this rule holds: that one never fails to do what one wants, when one can. Now this consequent will—final and decisive—results from the conflict of all the antecedent wills, both those that tend toward the good and those that repel evil; and it is from the concurrence of all these particular wills that the total will emerges. This is much like in **mechanics**, where a compound motion results from all the different tendencies that meet in the same moving body, and satisfies each equally as much as it is possible to do all at once. It is as if the moving body were divided between these tendencies, according to what I showed previously in one of the **Paris Journals** <note>Specifically the *Journal des Sçavans* from September 7, 1693.</note> when providing the general law of the **composition of motion**. And it is also in this sense that one can say that the antecedent will is effective in some way, and even successful in its result.

23. From this, it follows that God wills the good antecedently, and the best consequently. And as for evil, God does not will moral evil <term>Moral Evil: Sin or wickedness resulting from the choices of free beings.</term> at all, and he does not will physical evil <term>Physical Evil: Suffering, pain, or misfortune.</term> or suffering in an absolute manner. This is why there is no absolute Predestination to damnation. One can say of physical evil that God often wills it as a penalty due to guilt <note>original: "coulpe"</note>, and often also as a means suited to an end—that is to say, to prevent greater evils or to obtain greater goods. Punishment also serves for reform and as an example; and evil often serves to allow us to better taste the good, and sometimes it even contributes to a greater perfection in the one who suffers it, just as the grain that is sown must undergo a kind of corruption in order to sprout. This is a beautiful comparison which Jesus Christ used himself <note>Leibniz refers to John 12:24: "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit."</note>.

24. As for sin or moral evil, although it also very often happens that it may serve as a means to obtain a good or to prevent another evil, this is not, however, what makes it a sufficient object of the divine will, or a legitimate object of a created will. It must only be admitted or permitted insofar as it is regarded as a certain consequence of an indispensable duty; so that he who would refuse to permit the sin of another would himself fail in his own duty. It is like an Officer who is tasked with guarding an important post: if he were to abandon it, especially in a time of danger, merely to prevent a quarrel in the city between two soldiers of the garrison who were ready to kill each other, he would be failing in his primary obligation.

25. <meta>This page continues Leibniz’s argument regarding the permission of evil. He is finishing a comparison (begun on page 90) between a human ruler's duty and God's supreme wisdom, explaining that while a human cannot justify a crime to save a state, God permits evil only because it is an unavoidable part of the best possible universe.</meta>

<page-num>91</page-num>
<header>AND THE FREEDOM OF MAN. PART I.</header>
<meta>catchword: not</meta>

...not that a Queen should claim to save the State by committing or even by permitting a crime. The crime is certain, and the harm to the State is doubtful; besides, if this way of authorizing crimes were accepted, it would be worse than the occasional upheaval of a country, which happens often enough on its own, and would perhaps happen more frequently by the very means chosen to prevent it. But with respect to God, nothing is doubtful; nothing could be opposed to *the rule of the best*, which allows for no exception or dispensation. And it is in this sense that God permits sin; for He would fail in what He owes to Himself—to His wisdom, His goodness, and His perfection—if He did not follow the grand result of all His tendencies toward the good, and if He did not choose that which is absolutely the best, notwithstanding the evil of guilt <note>original: "coulpe"; referring to the moral responsibility or fault of the sinner</note> that is wrapped up in it by the supreme necessity of eternal truths. From this, we must conclude that God wills all good in itself *antecedently* <gloss>Willing something "antecedently" means God desires it in isolation, based on its own merit.</gloss>, that He wills the best *consequently* <gloss>Willing something "consequently" means God chooses it as the final result after weighing all possible factors.</gloss> as an *end*, and that He wills indifferent things and physical evil sometimes as a *means*; but He wills only to permit moral evil as a *sine qua non* <note>original: "sine quo non"; a Latin phrase meaning "without which not," indicating a necessary condition.</note> or by a hypothetical necessity which binds it to the best. This is why the *consequent will* of God, which has sin as its object, is only permissive.

26. It is also worth considering that moral evil is only such a great evil because it is a source of physical evils, occurring in a creature that is among the most powerful and most capable of causing them. # AND THE LIBERTY OF MAN. PART I.
<sig>E 2</sig>
<meta>The catchword "pelle" at the bottom of the page likely refers to the word "appelle" (calls) appearing at the start of page 100.</meta>

future will be, just as it is certain that the past has been. It was already true a hundred years ago that I would be writing today; just as it will be true a hundred years from now that I have written. Thus, a <term>contingent</term> <note>In philosophy, "contingent" refers to something that happens but did not *have* to happen by logical necessity; the opposite of a "necessary" truth like 2+2=4.</note> event does not become any less contingent simply by being in the future. The *determination*—which we would call *certainty* if it were known—is not incompatible with contingency. One often mistakes the *certain* and the *determined* for the same thing, because a determined truth is in a state of being able to be known; thus, one could say that *determination* is an "objective certainty."

37. This determination arises from the very nature of truth itself and cannot harm liberty. However, there are other types of determination derived from other sources, primarily from the <term>prescience</term> <note>God's foreknowledge; the ability to know events before they happen.</note> of God, which many have believed to be contrary to liberty. For they say that what is foreseen cannot fail to exist—and they speak the truth—but it does not follow from this that the event is *necessary*. This is because a *Necessary Truth* is one whose opposite is impossible or implies a contradiction <note>For example, "a circle is round" is a necessary truth because a "square circle" is a logical contradiction. Leibniz argues that most human actions are not like this.</note>. Now, the truth which holds that "I will write tomorrow" is not of this nature; it is therefore not "necessary." 

But, assuming that God foresees it, it is necessary that it happens; that is to say, the *consequence* is necessary—namely, that it exists because it has been foreseen, for God is infallible. This is what is called a <term>hypothetical necessity</term> <note>A necessity that depends on a condition. For example: *If* I am running, then it is necessarily true that I am moving. But "running" itself is not a necessary state for me to be in.</note>; but this is not the type of necessity we are discussing here. It is an <term>absolute necessity</term> that is required for one to be able to say that an action is not contingent or is not the result of a free choice. Furthermore, it is very easy to judge that foreknowledge in itself adds nothing to the determination of the truth of future contingents, other than the fact that this determination is known. This does not increase the determination, or the <term>futurition</term> <note>original: "futurition"; a technical term used in scholastic philosophy to describe the state of an event being in the future.</note> (as it is called)...

<summary>Leibniz argues that God’s foreknowledge of the future (prescience) does not take away human freedom, because an event can be "certain" to happen without being logically "necessary." He distinguishes between absolute necessity and hypothetical necessity to show that our choices remain free even if God knows them in advance.</summary>

38. This response is undoubtedly very just; it is agreed that <term>foreknowledge</term> <note>original: "prescience"; the ability to know things before they happen.</note> in itself does not make a truth more determined: an event is foreseen because it is determined, or because it is true; but it is not true simply because it is foreseen. In this regard, knowledge of the future is no different from knowledge of the past or the present. However, here is what an opponent might say: I grant you that foreknowledge in itself does not make the truth more determined, but the *cause* of that foreknowledge does. For God's foreknowledge must surely have its foundation in the nature of things, and this foundation—by making the truth *predetermined*—prevents it from being contingent and free.

39. It is this difficulty that gave rise to two parties: the *Predeterminists*, and the defenders of *middle knowledge*. The <term>Dominicans</term> and <term>Augustinians</term> <note>Two influential Catholic religious orders. In these debates, they generally emphasized God's sovereign power and the idea that God moves the human will directly.</note> are in favor of predetermination; the <term>Franciscans</term> and modern <term>Jesuits</term> are more in favor of <term>middle knowledge</term> <note>Also called "scientia media," this is the theory that God knows what any free creature would do in any given set of circumstances, allowing for both divine foresight and human choice.</note>. These two parties emerged toward the middle of the sixteenth century and slightly later. <term>Molina</term> <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600), a Spanish Jesuit whose theories attempted to reconcile grace and free will.</note> himself (who is perhaps one of the first, along with <term>Fonseca</term>, to have organized this point into a system, and for whom the others were called <term>Molinists</term>) says in the book he wrote on *The Harmony of Free Will with Grace* <note>original: "la concorde du libre arbitre avec la grace"</note>, around the year 1570, that the Spanish Doctors (referring mainly to the <term>Thomists</term> <note>Followers of the theology of St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>) who had written over the previous twenty years, finding no other way to explain how God could have a certain knowledge of future contingent events, had introduced predeterminations as necessary to free actions.
