We are given the famous example of David, who asks the divine Oracle if the inhabitants of the city of Keilah <note>original: "Kegila"; see 1 Samuel 23.</note>, where he intended to take refuge, would deliver him to Saul in the event that Saul besieged the city. God answered yes, and based on that, David took another path. Now, some defenders of this "science" consider that God, orseeing what men would freely do if they were placed in such or such circumstances, and knowing they would make bad use of their free will, decrees to refuse them graces and favorable circumstances. He can decree this justly, since these circumstances and aids would have been of no use to them anyway. But Molina is content to find there a general reason for God's decrees, based on what the free creature would do in such or such circumstances.

# ESSAYS ON THE GOODNESS OF GOD,
## THE LIBERTY OF MAN, AND THE ORIGIN OF EVIL.

Some claim that *middle knowledge* <note>original: "science moyenne"; the theory that God knows what any free creature would do in any given circumstance.</note> must be included within the *knowledge of simple intelligence* <note>original: "science de simple intelligence"; God's pure understanding of all possibilities, regardless of whether they ever happen.</note>. However, the main objection is directed against the very foundation of this knowledge. For what foundation could God have for seeing what the inhabitants of Keilah <note>original: "Kegilites"; referring to the biblical story in 1 Samuel 23 where David asks if the citizens of Keilah would betray him to Saul.</note> would do? A simple contingent and free act has nothing in itself that could provide a principle of certainty, unless it is considered as *predetermined* <note>The idea that an event is fixed in advance by preceding causes or divine decree.</note> by the decrees of God and by the causes that depend on them. Therefore, the difficulty found in actual free actions will also be found in conditional free actions; that is to say, God will only know them under the condition of their causes and His decrees, which are the primary causes of things. And one cannot detach these actions from their causes to know a contingent event in a manner independent of the knowledge of those causes. Thus, everything would have to be reduced to the predetermination of God's decrees; therefore, this middle knowledge (it will be argued) will remedy nothing. The theologians who claim to be followers of Saint Augustine also argue that the approach of the *Molinists* <note>Followers of Luis de Molina, who sought to protect human free will by limitng God's direct control over every choice.</note> would place the source of God's grace in the good qualities of man, which they judge to be contrary to the honor of God and the doctrine of Saint Paul.

42. It would be long and tedious to enter here into the replies and rejoinders made by both sides; it will suffice for me to explain how I conceive that there is truth on both sides. To this end, I turn to my principle of an infinity of *possible worlds*, represented in the region of eternal truths—that is, in the object of Divine Intelligence—where all conditional futures must be included. For the case of the Siege of Keilah concerns a *possible world, which differs from ours only in everything connected to that hypothesis*, and the idea of this possible world represents <meta>catchword: what (ce)</meta>

44. However, objective certainty or determination does not at all constitute the necessity of the determined truth. To better understand this point, one must consider that there are two great principles of our reasoning: one is the **principle of contradiction**, which holds that of two contradictory propositions, one is true and the other false; the other principle is that of **determining reason** <note>Known today as the Principle of Sufficient Reason—the idea that everything happens for a specific reason, even if we don't know it.</note>. Without this great principle, we could never prove the **existence of God**, and we would lose an infinity of very just and very useful reasonings of which it is the foundation: and it suffers no exception, otherwise its force would be weakened. 45. One must not, therefore, imagine—as do certain **Scholastics** <term>medieval philosophers and theologians who used highly structured, logical methods of inquiry</term> who indulge somewhat in fantasy—that free **future contingents** <note>Events that will happen in the future but are not logically necessary, such as a person's choice to go for a walk.</note> are exempt from this general rule of the nature of things. The will is never moved to act except by the representation of a good that prevails over contrary representations. This is agreed upon even regarding God, the good Angels, and blessed souls; and it is recognized that they are no less free for it. God does not fail to choose the best, but He is not at all constrained to do so; and indeed, there is no necessity in the object of God's choice, for another sequence of things is equally possible. This is precisely why the choice is free and independent of necessity: because it is made among several possibilities, and the will is determined only by the prevailing goodness of the object. Thus, this is not a defect in relation to God and the Saints; on the contrary, it would be a great defect, or rather a manifest absurdity, if it were otherwise—even in men here below—and if they were capable of acting without any inclining reason. One will never find an example of this; even when one takes a side out of caprice, to demonstrate one's freedom, the pleasure or advantage one expects to find in this display is one of the reasons that motivates it.

Everything is therefore certain and determined in advance in man, just as it is everywhere else, and the human soul is a species of ***spiritual automaton*** <term>spiritual automaton: Leibniz's concept that the soul follows its own internal laws of thought and desire, moving itself like a complex machine without needing constant external intervention</term>, even though contingent actions in general, and free actions in particular, are not for that reason necessary with an **absolute necessity**, which would indeed be incompatible with contingency. Thus, neither the **futurity** <term>futurition: the quality of being a future event; the fact that something will happen</term> in itself, certain as it is, nor the infallible foresight of God, nor the predetermination of causes, nor that of God's decrees, destroys this contingency and this liberty. This is agreed upon regarding futurity and foresight, as has already been explained; and since God's decree consists solely in the resolution he takes—after having compared all **possible Worlds**—to choose the one which is the best, and to admit it into existence by the almighty word ***Fiat*** <note>original: "Fiat"; Latin for "Let it be done"</note>, with everything that this World contains; it is clear that this decree changes nothing in the constitution of things. It leaves them just as they were in the state of pure possibility; that is to say, it changes nothing in their essence or nature, nor even in their **accidents** <term>accidents: in philosophy, these are non-essential properties of a thing, such as its color or a temporary action, which can change without the thing becoming something else</term>, which were already perfectly represented in the idea of this possible world. Thus, what is contingent and free remains no less so under God's decrees than under his foresight.

Thus, everything having been regulated from the start, it is only this **hypothetical necessity** <term>hypothetical necessity: a type of certainty where something must happen only because of a prior condition (like God’s foresight), rather than being logically impossible for it to be otherwise</term>—which everyone agrees upon—that ensures that after God’s foresight or after His resolution, nothing can be changed: and yet, events in themselves remain **contingent** <term>contingent: describes an event that happens but could have theoretically been different; its opposite does not imply a logical contradiction</term>. For (setting aside this supposition of the **futurition** <term>futurition: the state of being "in the future" or the certainty that something will happen</term> of the thing and of God's foresight or resolution—a supposition which already takes as fact that the thing will happen, and after which one must say: *Everything, when it is, must necessarily be; or everything, if it will be, must necessarily be in the future* <note>original Latin: "Unumquodque, quando est, oportet esse, aut unumquodque, siquidem erit, oportet futurum esse"</note>), the event has nothing in itself that makes it necessary, or that prevents us from conceiving that something else could have happened in its place. And as for the connection between causes and effects, it only inclined the **free agent** without necessitating him, as we have just explained; thus, it does not even create a hypothetical necessity, unless one adds something from the outside, namely this very maxim: that the prevailing inclination always succeeds.

54. It will also be said that if everything is regulated, God therefore cannot perform **miracles**. Those actions that happen in this actual world were represented in the idea of this same world while it was still only possible, along with their effects and their consequences; they were represented there, drawing upon God's grace—whether natural or supernatural—demanding punishments, and asking for rewards, just as it actually happens in this world after God has chosen it. Prayer and good action were, from that moment, an *ideal cause* or *ideal condition*; that is to say, an inclining reason that could contribute to God's grace or to a reward, just as it does now in an actual manner. And as everything in the world is linked together by wisdom, it is clear that God, foreseeing what would happen freely, also regulated the rest of things in advance based on that, or (which is the same thing) he chose this possible world where everything was regulated in this manner.

55. This consideration at the same time strikes down what was called by the Ancients the *lazy sophism* <note>original Greek: λόγος ἀργός (*logos argos*)</note> which concluded that one should do nothing: for (it was said) "if what I ask for is to happen, it will happen even if I do nothing; and if it is not to happen, it will never happen, no matter what trouble I take to obtain it." One could call this necessity—which one imagines in events when they are detached from their causes—*Turkish Fate* <note>original Latin: *Fatum Mahometanum*</note>, as I have already noted above, because it is said that a similar argument causes the Turks not to avoid places where the plague is ravaging. But the answer is ready: the effect being certain, the cause that will produce it is also certain; and if the effect happens, it will be by a proportionate cause. Thus your laziness will perhaps cause you...

There is a German proverb which says that death always wants to have a cause. And nothing is so true. This spontaneity <term>spontaneity: here meaning the soul's ability to initiate its own actions from within, rather than being pushed by external physical forces</term>, little known until now, which raises our command over our actions as much as is possible, is a consequence of the *System of Pre-established Harmony*, of which it is necessary to give some explanation here. The Scholastic Philosophers believed that there was a reciprocal physical influence between the body and the soul: but since it has been well considered that thought and extended matter have no link together, and that they are creatures that differ *entirely in kind* <note>original: "toto genere"</note>; several Moderns have recognized that there is no *physical communication* between the soul and the body, although the *metaphysical communication* always remains, which ensures that the soul and the body compose one and the same *subject* <term>subject: translated from the Latin "suppositum," referring to a single, complete individual being</term>, or what is called a *person*. This physical communication, if it existed, would mean that the soul would change the degree of speed and the line of direction of certain movements within the body, and *the other way around* <note>original: "vice versa"</note> the body would change the sequence of thoughts within the soul. But one cannot derive this effect from any notion conceived in the body or in the soul; although nothing is better known to us than the soul, since it is intimate to us—that is to say, intimate to itself.

60. Mr. Descartes wanted to find a compromise, and make part of the body's action depend on the soul. He believed he knew a rule of nature, which states, according to him, that the same quantity of motion is preserved in bodies. He did not judge it possible that the influence of the soul could violate this law of bodies, but he believed that the soul could nevertheless have the power to change the *direction* of the movements occurring in the body; much like a rider, although he gives no strength to the horse he mounts, nevertheless manages to govern it by directing that strength to whichever side he sees fit. 61. 62. These goods and evils happen only through the assistance of these means, and if these events were necessary, the means would form a part of the causes that made them necessary; since experience teaches us that often fear or hope prevents evil or advances good. This objection therefore differs in almost nothing from the lazy sophism that one opposes to the certainty, as well as to the necessity, of future events. 73. There is, however, a kind of justice and a certain sort of rewards and punishments which do not seem so applicable to those who would act by an absolute necessity, if there were such a thing. It is that kind of justice which has for its goal neither amendment <note>improvement or reform of the offender</note>, nor example, nor even the reparation of the evil. This justice is founded only on **fitness** <term>fitness: (French: *convenance*) a central Leibnizian concept where things are done because they are "fitting" or "appropriate" to the order of perfection and harmony, rather than just out of logical necessity</term> which demands a certain satisfaction for the expiation of a bad action. The **Socinians** <term>Socinians: a rationalist Christian sect that, among other things, denied the necessity of Christ’s satisfaction (atonement) to appease divine retributive justice</term>, **Hobbes**, and some others do not admit this punitive justice, which is properly **vindicative** <term>vindicative justice: from the Latin *iustitia vindicativa*, this refers to retributive justice—punishment given as a matter of desert or "righting the scales," rather than just to deter others</term>, and which God has reserved for Himself in many instances; but which He nonetheless communicates to those who have the right to govern others, and which He exercises through them, provided they act by reason and not by passion. The Socinians believe it to be without foundation; but it is always founded in a relationship of **fitness** <gloss>convenance</gloss>, which satisfies not only the offended party but also the Wise who see it, just as beautiful music or good architecture satisfies well-ordered minds. And the wise **Legislator** having threatened, and having, so to speak, promised a punishment, it belongs to His consistency not to leave the action entirely unpunished, even if the penalty no longer served to correct anyone. But even if He had promised nothing, it is enough that there is a **fitness** <gloss>convenance</gloss> which could have led Him to make this promise; since indeed the Wise man promises only what is fitting.

75. But we shall not occupy ourselves now with discussing a question more curious than necessary, since we have sufficiently shown that there is no such necessity in voluntary actions. ...it has already been noted in the past that the **Contra-Remonstrants** <term>Contra-Remonstrants: Also known as Gomarists, these were strict Calvinists who believed God decided who would be saved before even considering human sin or merit.</term> took the first side, and the **Remonstrants** <term>Remonstrants: Followers of Jacobus Arminius who argued that God’s decision to save someone is based on his foreknowledge of that person's future faith.</term> took the second. But to do justice to the subject, one must equally uphold, on one hand, the independence of God and the dependence of creatures; and on the other hand, the justice and goodness of God, which makes him "depend" upon himself—that is, upon his own will, his understanding, and his wisdom.

78. Some skilled and well-intentioned authors, wishing to represent the strength of the arguments of these two main parties in order to persuade them toward a mutual **Tolerance** <note>In this period, "Tolerance" referred to the formal recognition that different religious sects could coexist despite their disagreements on the mechanics of salvation.</note>, judge that the entire controversy reduces to this one vital point: namely, what was God's primary goal in making his **decrees** <term>Decrees of God: The eternal, unchangeable plans of God regarding the creation and the fate of the universe.</term> concerning man? Did he make them solely to establish his glory by manifesting his attributes, and by forming the great project of **providence** <term>Providence: God's intervention and guidance in the world.</term> and creation to achieve this? Or did he instead have regard for the voluntary movements of the **intelligent substances** <term>Intelligent substances: Beings capable of reason, such as humans or angels.</term> he intended to create, considering what they would want and do in the different circumstances and situations where he might place them, in order to make a suitable resolution based on that?

It seems to me that the two answers given to this great question, though presented as being opposed to one another, are easy to reconcile. Consequently, the parties would find themselves in fundamental agreement, without any need for "tolerance," if the matter were reduced simply to this point. In truth, when God formed the design to create the World, he aimed solely to manifest and communicate his perfections in the most effective manner, and in a way most worthy of his greatness, his wisdom, and his goodness. But this very aim led him to consider all the actions of creatures while they were still in the state of possibility, in order to form the most suitable project. 79. I do not know if there are perhaps still people who imagine that since God is the absolute master of all things, one can infer that everything outside of him is indifferent to him; that he regarded only himself without caring for others, and that he thus made some happy and others unhappy, without any cause, without choice, without reason. But to teach such things about God would be to strip him of wisdom and goodness. And it is enough for us to note that he regards himself, and neglects nothing that he owes to himself, for us to judge that he also regards his creatures, and that he employs them in the manner most conforming to order. For the more a great and good Prince cares for his glory, the more he will think of making his Subjects happy, even if he were the most absolute of all Monarchs, and even if his Subjects were born slaves—"bondmen" <term>Bondmen: Translated from the legal term *hommes propres*, referring to people bound to the land or subject to the absolute power of a lord.</term> (as the **jurists** <term>Jurists: Legal scholars and experts in law.</term> say)—people entirely submitted to arbitrary power. To demonstrate this simultaneity of the destinations or the Decrees in question, one must return to the explanation I have used more than once: that God, before decreeing anything, considered—among other possible sequences of events—the one He eventually approved. In the conception of this sequence, it is represented how the first parents <note>Adam and Eve.</note> sin and corrupt their posterity; how Jesus Christ redeems the Human Race; how some, aided by such-and-such Graces, arrive at final faith and salvation; and how others, with or without such or other Graces, do not arrive there at all, remaining in sin and being damned. God gives His approval to this sequence only after having entered into all its details; thus, He pronounces nothing definitive regarding those who will be saved or damned without having weighed everything and even compared it with other possible sequences. 

Thus, what He pronounces regards the entire sequence at once, for which He merely decrees existence. To save other men, or to save them in a different way, it would have been necessary to choose an entirely different general sequence, for everything is interconnected in each sequence. And in this way of understanding the matter—which is the most worthy of the Wisest Being, whose actions are as interconnected as possible—there would be only one single total Decree, which is that of creating such a World. This total Decree encompasses all particular decrees equally, without there being any priority or sequence among them; although, on the other hand, one might say that each particular act of <term>antecedent will</term> <note>In Leibniz's philosophy, this is God's initial desire for every individual good (like the salvation of everyone) before He weighs how they all fit together into a single world.</note>, which enters into the total result, has its own value and order in proportion to the good toward which that act inclines. ...in man, not only does the soul subsist, but personality as well; that is to say, by saying the human soul is immortal, one maintains that which makes it the same person, which keeps its moral qualities by preserving ***Consciousness*** or the internal reflective feeling of what it is; this is what makes the soul capable of punishment and reward. But this preservation of personality has no place in the souls of beasts: that is why I prefer to say they are imperishable, rather than to call them immortal. However, this misunderstanding seems to have been the cause of a great inconsistency in the doctrine of the **Thomists** <note>Followers of the medieval theologian St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> and other good philosophers, who recognized the immateriality or indivisibility of all souls without wishing to admit their indestructibility, much to the detriment of the immortality of the human soul. **John Scotus**, that is to say "the Scot" (which formerly signified the Irishman or **Erigena** <note>Johannes Scotus Erigena (c. 815–877), a Neoplatonist philosopher. # ESSAYS ON THE GOODNESS OF GOD,

...the formation of animated organic bodies only seems explainable within the natural order if we assume an organic **preformation** <note>The biological theory, popular in the 17th and 18th centuries, that organisms develop from miniature versions of themselves already present in the sperm or egg.</note> is already present. From this, I have concluded that what we call the **generation** <note>The process of reproduction or birth.</note> of an animal is nothing more than a **transformation** and growth. Thus, because the body was already organized, we must believe it was already animated and possessed the same soul; just as I judge, conversely, concerning the preservation of the soul once it is created, that the animal is also preserved, and that apparent death is merely an enfolding. It is unlikely that within the order of nature there are souls entirely separated from all bodies, nor that anything which does not begin naturally can cease by the forces of nature.

91. Having established such a beautiful order and such general rules regarding animals, it does not seem reasonable that man should be entirely excluded from them, and that everything within him should occur by miracle in relation to his soul. I have also observed more than once that it is part of God’s wisdom that everything in His works be harmonious, and that nature should run parallel to grace. Thus, I believe that souls which will one day be **human souls**, like those of other species, were present in the seeds and in ancestors as far back as Adam, and have consequently existed since the beginning of things, always within some form of organized body. In this, it seems that Mr. **Swammerdam** <note>Jan Swammerdam (1637–1680), a Dutch biologist and microscopist.</note>, the Reverend Father **Malebranche** <note>Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715), a French Oratorian priest and philosopher.</note>, Mr. **Bayle** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), author of the influential *Historical and Critical Dictionary*.</note>, Mr. **Pitcairne** <note>Archibald Pitcairne (1652–1713), a Scottish physician.</note>, Mr. **Hartsoeker** <note>Nicolaas Hartsoeker (1656–1725), a Dutch mathematician and physicist who claimed to have seen "homunculi" in sperm.</note>, and many other highly skilled persons share my sentiment. This is all the easier to admit since **Revelation** <note>Divine truth as revealed through scripture or religious tradition.</note> teaches many other immediate operations of God upon our souls. This explanation seems to resolve the difficulties that arise here in philosophy or theology: for the difficulty regarding the **origin of forms** <note>A long-standing philosophical debate about how new souls or essences are created during reproduction.</note> ceases entirely; and it is far more fitting to Divine justice to give a soul—already physically or animally corrupted by **Adam’s sin**—a new perfection which is Reason, than to place a rational soul, created anew or otherwise, into a body where it must be corrupted *morally*.

# ESSAYS ON THE GOODNESS OF GOD,
<meta>catchword: hu-</meta>

When I speak here of damnation and hell, I mean actual suffering, and not merely a simple deprivation of supreme happiness; I mean the **punishment of the senses**, not merely the **punishment of loss** <note>original: *pœnam sensus, non damni*. In traditional theology, the "punishment of loss" is the spiritual pain of being separated from God, while the "punishment of the senses" refers to physical torment, such as fire.</note>. Gregory of Rimini, General of the Augustinians, along with a few others, followed St. Augustine against the accepted opinion of the Schools of his time; for this reason, he was called the **torturer of infants** <note>original: *tortor infantum*. This refers to his harsh view that unbaptized infants suffer physical torment in hell.</note>. The Scholastics <note>Medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note>, instead of sending them into the flames of hell, assigned them a specific **Limbo** <note>From the Latin word for "border," Limbo was theorized as a place for those who died without personal sin but also without baptism, thus residing on the edge of heaven and hell.</note>, where they do not suffer at all, and are punished only by being deprived of the **beatific vision** <note>The direct, eternal sight and knowledge of God, considered the highest possible happiness.</note>. The *Revelations of Saint Bridget* (as they are called), which are highly esteemed in Rome, also support this doctrine. Salmeron and Molina, following Ambrosio Catarino and others, grant them a certain natural happiness; and Cardinal Sfondrat—a man of learning and piety who approves of this—recently went so far as to somewhat prefer their state (which is a state of happy innocence) to that of a saved sinner. This can be seen in his work, *The Knot of Predestination Untied* <note>original: *Nodus prædestinationis solutus*.</note>. However, it seems this goes a bit too far: it is true that a soul properly enlightened would never wish to sin, even if it could obtain all imaginable pleasures by that means; but the choice between sin and true happiness is a purely imaginary scenario, and it is better to obtain happiness (even after a period of repentance) than to be deprived of it forever.

93. Many Prelates and Theologians in France, who are happy to distance themselves from Molina and attach themselves to St. Augustine, seem to lean toward the opinion of that great Doctor, who condemns to eternal flames children who die in the age of innocence before having received baptism. <header>AND THE FREEDOM OF MAN. PART I.</header>

He told us then that what had contributed greatly to determining his move to the side of the **Roman Church** was the voice of a Lady in **Florence**, who had shouted to him from a window: *do not go the way you want to go, Sir, go the other way.* This voice struck me (he told us) because I was in meditation on Religion at that moment. This Lady knew that he was looking for a man in the house where she was, and seeing him take one path for another, she wanted to show him the way to his friend's room.

101. The Jesuit Father **Jean Davidius** <note>Jan David (1545–1613), a Flemish Jesuit author.</note> wrote a book entitled *The Veracious Christian* <note>original: "Veridicus Christianus"</note>, which is like a kind of **bibliomancy** <term>bibliomancy: the practice of seeking spiritual guidance by opening a book—usually the Bible—to a random page and interpreting the first passage seen as a divine message</term>, where one takes passages at random, following the example of the *Take up and read* <note>original: "Tolle, Lege"</note> of **St. Augustine**; it is like a game of devotion. But the hazards in which we find ourselves despite ourselves contribute only too much to what gives or takes away salvation from men. Let us imagine two **Polish** twin children, one taken by the **Tatars**, sold to the **Turks**, led into apostasy, plunged into impiety, dying in despair; the other saved by some chance, later falling into good hands to be properly instructed, permeated by the most solid truths of Religion, practiced in the virtues it recommends, dying with all the feelings of a good Christian: one will pity the misfortune of the first, whom a small circumstance perhaps prevented from being saved as well as his brother; and one will be astonished that this small hazard should have decided his fate in relation to eternity.

102. Someone will perhaps say that God foresaw through **middle knowledge** <term>middle knowledge: a theological concept (scientia media) suggesting God knows what any free creature would do in any given set of circumstances</term> that the first would also have been wicked and damned if he had remained in **Poland**. There are perhaps encounters in which something of this sort takes place. But will it then be said

<summary>Leibniz examines the profound impact of random life circumstances—such as a misdirected shout or being captured in war—on an individual's religious path and eternal salvation. He introduces the concept of "middle knowledge" to address whether God foresees how a person would act in different environments.</summary>

<header>ESSAYS ON THE GOODNESS OF GOD,</header>

Would this not contradict our Lord, who says that **Tyre** and **Sidon** <note>Ancient Phoenician cities mentioned in the Gospels (Matthew 11:21).</note> would have profited more from his preaching than **Capernaum**, if they had had the good fortune to hear it?

103. But even if one were to grant here this use of **middle knowledge** <term>middle knowledge: also known as *scientia media*, this is the theological concept that God knows how any free creature would choose to act in any possible set of circumstances</term> against all appearances, it still supposes that God considers what man would do in such or such circumstances. And it remains always true that God could have placed him in other, more salutary <note>beneficial to health or, in this case, the soul's salvation</note> ones, and given him internal or external help capable of overcoming the greatest depths of malice that might be found in a soul. I will be told that God is not obliged to do so, but that is not enough; one must add that greater reasons prevent him from making all his goodness felt by everyone. Thus there must be a choice, but I do not think that the reason for it should be sought absolutely in the good or bad nature of men. For if one supposes, as some do, that God—choosing the plan that produces the most good, but which involves sin and damnation—was led by his wisdom to choose the best natures to make them objects of his grace, it seems that the **Grace of God** will not be sufficiently gratuitous <note>original: "gratuite"; in this theological context, it means "freely given" by God's favor rather than earned through human merit</note>, and that man would distinguish himself by a kind of innate merit. This seems far removed from the principles of **St. Paul**, and even from those of **Supreme Reason**.

104. It is true that there are reasons for God’s choice, and the consideration of the object—that is to say, of man’s nature—must enter into it; but it does not appear that this choice can be subjected to a rule that we are capable of conceiving, and which could flatter the pride of men.

<meta>catchword: Some-</meta>

<summary>Leibniz argues that salvation is not merely a result of a person's innate nature, as this would make divine grace a reward for merit rather than a free gift. He contends that while God has reasons for His choices, they are rooted in a supreme wisdom that surpasses human understanding and avoids favoring human pride.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distribution of divine grace. The previous page ended with the suggestion that God’s choice in providing grace might be driven by a higher wisdom rather than simply by a person’s inherent nature. This page explores whether God favors those who are "less resistant" and how individual differences fit into the grand design of the universe.</meta>

->AND THE LIBERTY OF MAN. PART I.<-

G 3

Some famous theologians believe that God offers more graces, or offers them in a more favorable manner, to those whom he foresees will resist less, and that he abandons the others to their own stubbornness. There is reason to believe that this is often the case, and this approach—among those who argue that man distinguishes himself by what is favorable in his own nature—is the one that moves furthest away from **Pelagianism** <term>Pelagianism: a theological doctrine that emphasizes human free will and suggests that people can take the initial steps toward salvation without divine grace; it was historically condemned as heresy.</term>. However, I would not dare to make this a universal rule. And so that we have no reason to boast, we must remain ignorant of the reasons for God’s choice. These reasons are far too varied to fall within our understanding, and it is possible that God sometimes shows the power of his grace by overcoming the most stubborn resistance, so that no one has cause to despair, just as no one should have cause to flatter themselves. It seems that **Saint Paul** held this thought, presenting himself as an example in this regard: God, he says, showed me mercy to give a great example of his patience <note>Paraphrase of 1 Timothy 1:16: "But for that very reason I was shown mercy so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display his immense patience."</note>.

105. Perhaps, at the core, all men are equally bad, and consequently unable to distinguish themselves by their own good or less-bad natural qualities; but they are not bad in the same way. For there is an original, individual difference between souls, as **pre-established harmony** <term>pre-established harmony: the philosopher Leibniz’s concept that God synchronized all substances (like the soul and the body) at the moment of creation so they function together perfectly without actually influencing one another.</term> demonstrates. Some are more or less inclined toward a certain good or a certain evil, or toward their opposites, all according to their natural dispositions. But the general plan of the **Universe** which God has chosen for superior reasons causes men to find themselves in different circumstances. Those who encounter circumstances more favorable to their nature will more easily become the least wicked, the most virtuous, and the happiest—but always through the assistance of the impressions of grace.

<meta>catchword: in-</meta>

<summary>Leibniz argues that while God may favor those who are naturally less resistant to grace, His choices remain a divine mystery to prevent human pride. He suggests that individual differences and life circumstances are part of a vast, pre-established harmony designed by God.</summary>
<keywords>divine grace, Pelagianism, Saint Paul, pre-established harmony, natural disposition, human nature, divine choice, providence</keywords>

# ESSAYS ON THE GOODNESS OF GOD.

internal grace that God joins to it. It even happens sometimes in the course of human life that a more excellent nature succeeds less, for lack of cultivation or opportunities. One could say that men are chosen and arranged not so much according to their excellence, as according to the suitability they have within the **plan of God**; just as it is possible that one might use a lesser-quality stone in a building or in an assortment, because it happens to be the one that fills a certain void.

106. But finally, all these attempts at reasoning—where one does not need to fixate entirely on specific **hypotheses**—serve only to make us conceive that there are a thousand ways to **justify the conduct of God**: and that all the inconveniences we see, all the difficulties one might raise, do not prevent us from reasonably believing (even if we did not know it otherwise through demonstration <note>By "demonstration," the author refers to a logical or mathematical proof that leaves no room for doubt.</note>, as we have already shown and as will appear even more in what follows) that there is nothing so elevated as the **wisdom** of God, nothing so just as his judgments, nothing so pure as his **holiness**, and nothing more immense than his **goodness**.

It asserts that while human reason may not fully grasp every detail, God's ultimate wisdom, justice, holiness, and goodness remain beyond reproach.</summary>
